lesson.title: The Crash of 2008
lesson.summary: A collapse of the U.S. housing market and financial system in 2007 and 2008 triggered the worst economic crisis since the Great Depression, exposing risks that had built up over decades of financial deregulation and innovation.
lesson.body:
Through the early and mid 2000s, home prices across the United States climbed steadily, fueled in part by lenders who issued increasingly risky subprime mortgages, home loans made to borrowers with weak credit histories who often could not have qualified under older, stricter lending standards. Banks packaged thousands of these mortgages together into complex investments called mortgage backed securities and collateralized debt obligations, which were then sold to investors around the world, often with high safety ratings from credit rating agencies that badly misjudged the underlying risk.

This kind of financial engineering was made easier by years of deregulation, including the 1999 Gramm Leach Bliley Act, passed during the Clinton administration, which tore down parts of the wall the Glass Steagall Act had built in 1933 between commercial banking and riskier investment banking. That deregulation fit the broader spirit of Clinton era globalization, a confidence that freer markets and fewer restrictions would keep fueling American prosperity, but it also let banks take on debt and risk at a scale that regulators struggled to monitor.

When housing prices stopped rising and began to fall starting around 2006, homeowners increasingly defaulted on mortgages they could not afford, and the securities built on those mortgages lost value rapidly, spreading losses through banks and investment firms that held them. The crisis reached a breaking point in September 2008, when the major investment bank Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, still the largest bankruptcy in American history, and the insurance giant AIG required an emergency federal bailout to avoid collapse. Credit markets froze as banks stopped trusting each other enough to lend, threatening to bring the broader economy to a halt.

The scale of the crisis echoed older American anxieties, going back to the concentrated corporate power of the Gilded Age's rise of big business, about financial institutions that had grown too large and too interconnected to fail without dragging down the whole economy. Congress passed the Troubled Asset Relief Program in October 2008, authorizing roughly 700 billion dollars to stabilize banks, and the Federal Reserve took extraordinary emergency actions to keep credit flowing. Even so, the resulting Great Recession threw millions of Americans out of work, with unemployment eventually peaking near ten percent in late 2009, and millions of families lost homes to foreclosure. The crisis dominated the final months of the Bush presidency and became the central inheritance handed to the incoming administration after the 2008 election.
